sections.text: Lord Shri Krishna replied: When a man has given up the desires of his heart and is satisfied with the Self alone, be sure that he has reached the highest state.
The sage, whose mind is unruffled in suffering, whose desire is not roused by enjoyment, who is without attachment, anger or fear - take him to be one who stands at that lofty level.

He who wherever he goes is attached to no person and to no place by ties of flesh; who accepts good and evil alike, neither welcoming the one nor shrinking from the other - take him to be one who is merged in the Infinite.

We had been discussing chapter two, Sankhya Yoga, the Yoga of Knowledge. So far we have seen that this chapter is divided into four segments. In the first few verses, Arjuna says, I am Navirsheshya.
I dont know what to do. You tell me without any option what is good for me. Second, we have seen how Bhagavan responded. He said, you shouldnt be worried about anything that is happening in this world simply because what you see happening is temporary.
Theres nothing in this world which is permanent, because all your experiences are the senses coming in contact with the sense objects. That which you are worried about -- yourself -- is immortal. There is no death for it, there is no birth for it.
So is the case for his self, her self, my self. Therefore there is no worry about the self. Everything else is temporary.
So why worry about that? That was the knowledge part. And then he said: how to practice that? Now, just knowing that does not make your life easier. Just because I went to Gita class does not make my life easier on Monday through Friday.
What you should do is act just like you were acting before -- but establish yourself in yoga. Yoga is the equanimity of mind. When you establish your mind in equanimity, things will continue to change outside, but I will remain the same in dealing with them, whether they are conducive or inconducive. Samatvam Yoga Uchate -- equanimity of mind is Yoga.
When do I know that my mind is equanimous? When you become skillful in your actions. When your actions become crystallized and precise and efficient, you should know that you have established yourself in Yoga. Samatvam Yoga Uchate and Yoga Karmasu Kaushalam.
So one is the definition, and there is actually a test. If your actions are haphazard, even though you think you are in yoga, you are not. Because a yogis actions will be all precise and dexterous.
Many times in my life I have seen this. The teaching says something that seems absolutely ridiculous, that its not going to happen. Somehow it all falls into place.
When I think from my logic, it should not work at all. But for him, if he says this should happen by this time and you should do this -- it happens. Because he has the mind of a yogi who can see through how to get things done.
Mine is the mind of a Bhogi who cannot see how this can ever happen. So Bhagavan said, thats your test. Yoga Karmasu Kaushalam. When we practice something over and over and over again, we become so efficient.
I used to practice music. My teacher said, keep practicing. You will get it before you even know when you got it.
You will never know the exact moment when you mastered it. But then you will know what is the Madhya Sapta, the Mantra Sapta, the Taar Sapta. Practice makes you perfect.
Once you achieve that art, you dont have to make any effort. Like driving -- thats Karmasu Kaushalam. I dont have to make any effort.
I dont even think about it while driving. Because I have achieved Karmasu Kaushalam, I am established in the yoga of driving. Therefore, Bhagavan says, thats what equanimity of mind means.
But we come to this conclusion very quickly that this is not possible -- this is just for great yogis like Buddha and Mahavir, not for us. So the question arises: okay, if thats the case, how do we know that someone is established in yoga? So Arjuna asked the question about this Prajna which is Sthita -- whose intellect is steady. We saw the definition: Samatvam Yoga Uchate.
Once ones intellect becomes steady, he becomes Sthita Prajna -- because that Prajna is not changing no matter what the outside situation is. It may be very dark in this room, but I know it is daytime. Because my prajna is sthita in the knowledge that it is daytime right now.
Even if you turn off light, even if there is clouds outside and it becomes very dark, I still say its daytime. Because I know it is daytime. Because my prajna is completely sthida in that knowledge.
The knowledge which Bhagavan gave in the first section that you are not the mortal being, you are the immortal being. Your self is immortal. Everything else is just passing experiences.
Once that knowledge takes place in the intellect, no matter what happens in my life, it does not change my understanding of that fact. If that happens to somebody who establishes himself in that knowledge, what is the description of such a person? How would I know such a person? So Arjuna in verse 54 asked that question. Sthita Prajnasya Ka Bhasha Samadhisthasya Keshava.
We know Samadhistha -- one who is established in Samadhi. Sama + Dhi: Buddhi which is steady. We use this word Samadhi in a very metaphysical way, but Samadhi is simply a firm conviction that this is the reality.
In one Upanishad class we were told that you are in a complete state of Samadhi right now -- of your body consciousness. Nobody has to remind me who I am. No matter what situation changes.
Outside, it is dark, it is light. If everybodys here, nobodys here. This is me that never changes.
You can convince me, if you are persuasive enough that this class does not exist. I am just hallucinating. Rajan, you need some help. You are hallucinating.
Youre talking to yourself. Its possible that I will believe that and will start seeking advice. But you cant convince me that I dont exist. No matter how confused I am, you cant convince me that I dont exist.
But what Bhagavan is saying is that this self is actually immortal, not this body. So therefore you shouldnt be worried about death. Your samadhi should be in this immortality.
So Arjuna asks: Bhagavan, how would that person who is established in the samadhi of his immortal self behave? His intellect is so steady that no matter what happens, he never loses that connection with that Samadhi. What is his description? To speak, Bhasa is describing. Thats why the language is called Bhasha.
Because we describe what we think through our speech. So what is his description of such a person? Great teachers get this question all the time., are you realized?, there is a conundrum here. If I tell you that I am realized, then what would you say? He tells everybody hes realized.
Now if Im not realized, why am I wasting time with you? If after all this, you are not realized, what am I going to get out of you? So there is no way to find out one is realized or not. Only another Realized person will know who this realized person is, one who is a good singer. If somebody sings, he knows hes a good singer.
For us, everybody is a good singer. But one who really knows music, he knows when the other person is doing well or not. So Arjuna said, how would I know that such a person exists? Or this can be achievable.
Give me some description, give me some idea. And now all I can do is judge people by how they behave, right? I cant really go into their mind and say they are established in samadhi, but I can see from their behavior. Therefore, the second line says, sthita dihi Kim Prabhasheta Kim Asita Vrajeta Kim.
This is indicative of knowing how a person with that level of establishment in Yoga will be behaving in this world. How does he walk, how does he sit? Prabha cheta talk Kim Asita. How does he sit down and how does he walk? Basically, in indicative words, to know what would be his outward behavior.
Now our problem is, once we know the outward behavior, somebody says, somebody will be sitting like this, somebody will be talking like that, somebody will be doing like that. Now we are trying to see that in a person and then basically come to the conclusion he is not. Because he is not fitting into my description of how Sthita Pragna should be a muni.
He should be sitting. So our idea of muni is sitting in Himalaya somewhere who is completely secluded from people, not interacting with people, not getting emotionally upset or emotionally charged with any situation. So well say, I dont know about that teacher.
One still gets angry. And it says that Vitaraga Bhayakrodha is still angry. The answer was, if I go to the ocean and try to see the ocean in a wave, and if I only see the characteristics of the wave, only thing I will see is the wave.
Only never see the ocean in the wave, the wave its own characteristics. If Im focusing on those characteristics, I only see wave in it. But if I see that the wave is nothing but the ocean rising and falling, I will see the ocean in it.
So Arjuna wants to know, how do I know that a person like that exists? Tell me some description, give me some idea. How will he behave in any situation? This is more like that bracelet these Christians have for the teenager, says wwjd what would Jesus do? This was, I think, a brilliant idea. Whoever came up with that, the teenagers, when they are in a dilemma, in some peer Press in school or whatever.
What should I do when everybodys asking me to smoke? But my parents say youre not supposed to smoke. He said, look at that person. WWJD what would Jesus do in this situation? How do I know what to do in a situation Im encountering? How would a realized person would act in this situation? So the answer comes in the following verses till the end of the chapter.
What a realized person will do in different situations. Once your mind is steady, your excellence will be effortless. And then you will know in each situation how to react to that situation.
Things and beings outside will continue to remain exactly as they are. As the Prakriti says, constantly changing. How would I react will change if my mind is equanimous.
So thats basically the gist of this question. So the answer is Prajahati Yada Kaman Sarvan Partha Manogatan. The first thing: who has given up all the desires? Sarvan Kaman Manogatan is the operative word -- desires born out of my mental agitations.
One who gives up all the desires born out of the mind. What is our primordial desire? To be happy. I want to be comfortable and happy.
But out of this primordial desire to be happy, all other desires have come into this one. If I didnt have that desire to be happy and be okay with any situation, it looks like the guy is going to be a stone. A dead person who has no reaction to anything good or bad.
It can only happen when I die. After I die, people can kick me. Im fine, put me and throw me in a well.
Ill be fine because Im not there. But while Im leaving, Ill be very careful. So they say, is that person be any different than all of us? However, he will be different from you in this following manner.
Prajahati Yada Kaman Sarvan Manogatan. Right now I have decided that when I fulfill all these desires, Ill be happy. A realized person does not have those desires.
That does not mean that he does not become thirsty and wont have the desire to drink water. Actually, Tejomayananda and others categorize all the desires and say: these desires which you can fulfill easily, dont even bother about them. Why are you suffering? Thats not the Manogatan desires we are talking about.

Krishnas answer to What is a Sthitaprajna (person of steady wisdom)? begins here. Verse 55: When a man has given up the desires of his heart and is satisfied with the Self alone, be sure that he has reached the highest state. The key phrase is Manogatan - desires born from the mind, meaning fabricated wants rather than genuine needs. The Sthitaprajna is satisfied with the Self alone - finding completeness within rather than seeking it from external accomplishments or possessions.
Verse 56 describes behavioral signs: The sage, whose mind is unruffled in suffering, whose desire is not roused by enjoyment, who is without attachment, anger or fear - take him to be one who stands at that lofty level. This is not suppression of emotions but their natural absence when one is fulfilled within. Verse 57 adds: He who wherever he goes is attached to no person and to no place... who accepts good and evil alike, neither welcoming the one nor shrinking from the other - take him to be one who is merged in the Infinite.
Examine your own desires today. Which are genuine needs and which are Manogatan - fabricated by your mind, perhaps influenced by advertising, social comparison, or habit? Notice which desires, if fulfilled, would still leave you wanting more. The Sthitaprajna has discovered that no external acquisition brings lasting satisfaction - only recognizing ones inherent completeness does. As a practice, spend time today simply being - not doing, not acquiring, not accomplishing - and notice if you can touch a sense of sufficiency in that simple presence. This is the beginning of being satisfied with the Self alone.
